entries.text: ## Reading a vehicle's statistics  *(SR3 p.130–133)*

pdf.quote: The basic vehicle Attributes are Handling, Speed, Acceleration, Body, Armor, Signature, Autonav, Pilot, Sensor, Cargo Factor, Load, Seating and Entry Points

entries.note: The vehicle actor stores Handling (road and off-road), Speed, Accel, Body, Armor, Sig, Autonav, Pilot, Sensor, Cargo and Load, the attributes the book lists; Seating and Entry Points are separate fields.

entries.text: | Statistic | What it means |
entries.reason: table header row — states no rule

entries.text: | **Handling** | The base TN for Driving Tests, so **lower is better**. Most ground vehicles show two: **on road / off road**, as in 3/8. |

pdf.quote: The Handling Rating functions as the base target number for all Driving Tests that use a Vehicle Skill
higher the rating, the more difficult a vehicle is to control
the first represents the vehicle's Handling on a road, the second its Handling in off-road terrain

entries.note: Book (p.130): Handling is the base TN for every Driving Test; most ground vehicles have two ratings, the second used "in off-road terrain", and a ground vehicle off-road also halves its Speed. Code: the compendium vehicles carry both numbers (`handling`, `handlingOffRoad`) and the guide row is right, but every Driving Test, chase action and Crash Test reads only `handling.base` (SR3EVehicleSheet.js:1110, SR3EVehicleChase.js:817); `handlingOffRoad` is read nowhere in scripts/ (only declared in the data model and the character importer). So the off-road Handling is never used as the base TN, and the off-road Speed halving is not applied either.

entries.text: | **Speed** | Maximum safe speed, in **meters per Combat Turn**. A fixed-wing aircraft has two, its minimum and its maximum. |

pdf.quote: The Speed Rating represents the maximum safe speed at which a vehicle can travel for a sustained distance
Fixed-wing aircraft have two Speed Ratings. The higher number is its maximum safe speed; the lower represents the aircraft's stall speed

code.snippet: stallSpeed:   new NumberField({ integer: true, initial: 0, min: 0 }),

entries.note: Fixed in 0.7.0 (488f83b9): a vehicle has a stallSpeed field beside Speed; the packs store the HIGHER number as Speed (the maximum safe speed) and the lower as the stall speed for 29 aircraft, and the chase warns when an aircraft falls below its stall speed and offers the Crash Test (never rolled).

entries.text: | **Accel** | How much each success on a Driving Test can add to Speed in a chase. |

pdf.quote: increases the vehicle's Speed by its Acceleration Rating

entries.note: Accel is stored and shown, and the Collision tool's Braking Test uses it to slow a vehicle (Acceleration x successes, and the x4 deceleration limit; scripts/data/collisions.mjs `braking`), but the chase's Accel / Brake action only rolls the Driving Test: a success does not add Acceleration to the vehicle's Speed (the Speed in the chase is typed in by hand).

entries.text: | **Body** | Toughness. It also sets the number of weapon mounts. |

pdf.quote: A vehicle's Body Rating represents its mass and measures how much punishment it can take
A vehicle's Body Rating also indicates how many weapons can be mounted on it

entries.note: Body as toughness is used throughout (damage track, soak, ramming, collisions: e.g. SR3EVehicleChase.js:531, SR3ECollision.js:69), but nothing counts weapon mounts against Body: no hardpoint or firmpoint appears anywhere in scripts/.

entries.text: | **Armor** | Hardened armor: it stops any hit whose Power (after the vehicle's Body, but not counting burst or autofire) doesn't beat it. |

pdf.quote: deflect all damage from weapons with a Power (modified by the vehicle's Body, but not by burst or autofire) equal to or less than the Armor Rating

entries.note: Fixed in 0.7.0 (7a8bcb68): the attack carries hardenedPower (the weapon's own Power after the vehicle-mass halving, burst and full-auto bonus taken back off) and VehicleArmor.deflects compares that with the Armor Rating. The deflection is announced on the soak card, never applied.

entries.text: | **Sig** | Signature: the TN for sensors and guided weapons to lock on. |

pdf.quote: serves as the target number for sensor and missile to-hit tests made against the vehicle

entries.note: A vehicle weapon's base TN and the chase's Sensor/targeting tests default to the target vehicle's Sig.

entries.text: | **Autonav** | The collision-avoidance and navigation system, a driver's assistant. It can't fire weapons. |

pdf.quote: The autonav system serves as a driver's assistant. It can make minor control adjustments to avoid collisions and can navigate a course

code.snippet: const bonus    = usingVCR ? cpDice : (combatOn || collision ? 0 : autonav);

entries.note: Autonav adds dice to non-combat Driving Tests only. "It can't fire weapons" is the book's description and nothing in the code lets Autonav fire one.

entries.text: | **Pilot** | A drone's own brain. Ordinary vehicles have none (—). |

pdf.quote: The Pilot Rating indicates a drone's autonomous

entries.note: Pilot drives a drone's initiative and its own tests; the compendium vehicles store 0 for the book's "--".

entries.text: | **Sensor** | Detection, identification and targeting systems. |

pdf.quote: The Sensor Rating represents the vehicle's target-detection (knowing a target exists)

entries.note: Sensor is read for sensor-enhanced gunnery and the chase's sensor tests.

entries.text: | **Cargo** | Cargo Factor: each point is a cube half a meter on a side. |

pdf.quote: half a meter long on each side (0.125 cubic meters)

entries.note: Cargo Factor is stored and shown on the vehicle sheet; nothing computes with it.

entries.text: | **Load** | What it can carry, in kilograms. |

pdf.quote: Load represents the amount of cargo weight (in kilograms) a vehicle can lift, pull or carry

entries.note: Load is stored and shown on the vehicle sheet; nothing computes with it.

entries.text:
The full rules for each are summarized on
[Rigging](../rigging/#vehicle-attributes).

entries.text: ## Weapon mounts  *(SR3 p.307, p.312)*

pdf.quote: Fixed mounts fire in a fixed arc, and the weapon is permanently affixed to the mount

entries.note: Section heading; the mounts exist as gear items in the vehicle-mods pack. The mount RULES (units 64-67) are resolved individually below.

entries.text:
- **Hardpoints** carry heavy and vehicle weapons (MMGs and larger);
  **firmpoints** carry LMGs, assault rifles and smaller.

pdf.quote: Heavy and vehicular weapons (MMGs and larger) must be mounted on hardpoints; smaller arms (LMGs, assault rifles and smaller) may be mounted on firmpoints

entries.note: No hardpoint/firmpoint concept: any weapon item can be added to any vehicle's Weapons tab.

entries.text:
- A vehicle's **Body** sets how many it has: a hardpoint takes 2 points of
  Body, a firmpoint 1. A Body 4 vehicle could have 2 hardpoints, or a
  hardpoint and 2 firmpoints, or 4 firmpoints.

pdf.quote: Each hardpoint is worth 2 points of Body, and each firmpoint counts for 1 point

entries.note: Nothing counts mounts against Body; the Body 4 example (2 hardpoints, or a hardpoint and 2 firmpoints, or 4 firmpoints) cannot be checked by the system.

entries.text:
- **Firmpoints** are fixed mounts or pintle mounts; **hardpoints** are
  fixed mounts or turrets.

pdf.quote: Firmpoints can be a fixed mount or a pintle mount. Hardpoints can be a fixed mount or a turret.

entries.note: The fixed mount, pintle mount and turret exist as gear items; the rule that firmpoints take only fixed/pintle and hardpoints only fixed/turret is not modelled.

entries.text:
- **Fixed mounts** fire in a fixed arc, usually forward or back, and
  **halve recoil**, which cancels a heavy weapon's doubling. The driving
  rigger can fire them. A side-firing fixed mount adds its recoil to the
  vehicle's Handling and forces a Crash Test. External fixed mounts lower
  the Signature by 1.

pdf.quote: Fixed mounts reduce recoil modifiers by half (negating the double recoil modifier of heavy weapons)
Side-firing fixed mounts add their recoil to the vehicle's Handling Rating when fired; the driver must also make a Crash Test
External fixed mounts reduce the vehicle's Signature by 1

entries.note: None of the four effects (recoil halved, side-firing Handling and Crash Test, Signature -1, the rigger firing a fixed mount) is modelled; mounts are plain gear items.

> with a gas vent 3 and a shock pad, 4 points of compensation, and a laser
> sight (−1). Base TN 4 − 1 = **3**.

>   **3**, damage 8 + 3 = **11S**.
> - Burst two, 3 rounds at the second: 6 rounds fired, 2 uncompensated,
>   +2 for the second target. TN 3 + 2 + 2 = **7**, **11S**.
> - Burst three, 4 rounds at the third: 10 rounds, 6 uncompensated, +4 for
>   the third target. TN 3 + 6 + 4 = **13**, damage 8 + 4 = **12S**.

entries.text: ## Shotguns  *(SR3 p.117)*

pdf.quote: The shotguns described in the Street Gear section (beginning on p. 277) fire slug rounds.

entries.text:
The listed shotguns fire **slugs**. **Shot rounds** use the **flechette
rules** on the gun's Damage Code, and spread:

pdf.quote: To determine the damage done by shot rounds, apply the flechette ammunition rules to the Damage Code indicated for the weapon.

entries.text:
- Set the **choke** from 2 to 10. Every *choke* meters the shot travels, the
  pattern widens by a meter.

pdf.quote: The shotgun user can set his weapon's choke at anywhere from 2 to 10.
For every number of meters equal to the choke setting that the shot travels, it will spread one meter

entries.text:
- Each widening costs **1 Power** and gives the attacker **−1 TN**. At Power
  0 the shot is spent.

pdf.quote: Every time a shot round increases its spread, it loses 1 point of power. Every time the shot spreads, subtract -1 from the attacker's target number.
When the Power reaches 0, the shot is considered ineffective

code.snippet: return { spreads: s, power: -s, tn: -s, dodge: s };

entries.text:
- **Everyone in the spread is a target.** The attacker rolls once; each
  target dodges and resists against those successes, with **+1 Damage
  Resistance die** per other target in front of them.

pdf.quote: within the area of spread is con- sidered a valid target.
Award an additional die to the target's Damage Resistance Test for every other target within the spread in front of the target.

code.snippet: each gets +1 Damage Resistance die per other target in front of them

entries.note: Offered, not applied: the attack goes at one target; the card tells the GM that everyone in the spread is a valid target and gets +1 Damage Resistance die per other target in front. The extra dice are not added to any roll.

entries.text:
- A smartlink is worth **−1** with shot. Smart goggles and laser sights
  don't help.

pdf.quote: Shotguns equipped with smartlinks that fire shot rounds receive a -1 target number modifier. Shotguns get no benefits from smart goggles or laser sights.

entries.text:
## Doing it in The 2nd Chumming (Foundry)
{: #doing-it-in-the-2nd-chumming-foundry }
entries.reason: page title / table of contents / heading / table header row / category label / rule — states no rule

entries.text: ### Getting a weapon
entries.reason: page title / table of contents / heading / table header row / category label / rule — states no rule

entries.text:
Drag a weapon onto the character from the compendiums, or buy it with
**🛒 Buy gear**. It appears on the **Weapons** tab. Its category picks the
skill and the range bands; **Range override** on the weapon replaces the
bands, as "5/15/30/50".
entries.reason: describes the system's interface, not a book rule

entries.text: ### Shooting
entries.reason: page title / table of contents / heading / table header row / category label / rule — states no rule

entries.text:
- **✋** marks a weapon **ready** in hand; drawing one is a Ready Weapon
  action *(SR3 p.107)*.

pdf.quote: A character may ready a weapon by spending a Simple Action

code.snippet: /** ✋ Toggle ready. Readying is a Simple Action (charged if it is this
* ✋ In hand or put away (SR3 p.107, TODO 47) — only for weapons that c

entries.note: The ✋ toggle marks a weapon in hand; readying charges a Simple Action (Ready Weapon), putting away is free.

entries.text:
- The **🎲** on the row opens the attack. Choose the **fire mode** and, for
  full-auto, the rounds. The dialog shows the **range band** measured on the
  map, the **recoil** after compensation (the weapon's own and the
  character's, both editable), the target count for this phase, and every
  other modifier. The TN is yours to change before you roll.
entries.reason: describes the system's interface, not a book rule

entries.text:
- **Smartgun**, **laser sight** and **recoil compensation** are fields on the
  weapon. A smartgun saves the rounds walked fire would waste.
entries.reason: describes the system's interface, not a book rule

entries.text:
- A shotgun loaded with **shot** asks for the **choke**, and the card shows
  each spread's Power and TN.
entries.reason: describes the system's interface, not a book rule

entries.text: - **🎯** on the token's HUD fires a ready weapon from the map.
entries.reason: describes the system's interface, not a book rule

entries.text: ### Ammunition
entries.reason: page title / table of contents / heading / table header row / category label / rule — states no rule

entries.text:
- **↻ Reload** loads from ammunition on the character: loose rounds of the
  gun's class, or a spare clip. The loaded type (regular, APDS, explosive,
  gel, flechette, tracer, shot) changes the damage and the armor used on the
  soak card by itself.
entries.reason: describes the system's interface, not a book rule

entries.text:

entries.text:
{: .fixed }
> Original gist: "Cyberware Grades & Secondhand Gear Guide".
> - **Betaware is ×.6 Essence**, not ×.7.
> - **Used cyberware costs the Essence of its grade**, not ×1.25. It costs
>   **half price**, not ×.75.
> - The availability modifiers were invented. Alphaware is **as available as
>   basic**. Betaware is **+5 to the TN and ×1.5 the time**. Deltaware is at
>   least **+9 and ×3**. Used is standard.
> - **Betaware isn't available to starting characters** either, not only
>   deltaware.
> - Used deltaware **can't be bought**, but if you get hold of some, it can
>   be **installed as betaware**. It isn't "destroyed on extraction".
> - Used implants come with **1D3 permanent Stress Points**, not "1 to 2".
> - **Removing** chrome never gives Essence back. A *later* implant can use
>   the "Essence hole", but only through a surgical option at +2 Threshold.
> - The 1–3 hour harvest window, the TN 4–8 extraction roll and the
>   "Electronics (Cyberware) scrub" aren't in *Man & Machine*.

pdf.quote: Beta Delta Used -40% (x .6) 4 -50% (x .5) 8 By grade .5 +5/x 1.5 +9/x 3 Standard
Each used cyberware item comes with 1D3 permanent Stress Points

entries.note: Fixed for 0.6.1 (TODO 174). 'Betaware isn't available to starting characters' is still not enforced (no chargen flow to enforce it in).

entries.text: ## The four grades  *(M&M p.10–11)*

entries.text: - **Basic** is mass-market and fits anyone. Any street doc can install it.

pdf.quote: Any surgeon or street doctor can implant basic cyberware

  basic and costs twice as much.

pdf.quote: It is as readily available as basic cyberware, but it costs twice as much and also reduces Essence loss

  and uses myomers in place of gyros and microengines. It must be
  special-ordered.

pdf.quote: Betaware must be special-ordered

entries.text:
- **Deltaware** is built during the surgery itself, in corporate clinics
  that are almost never mentioned. It isn't available on the street.

entries.text: ## Selling harvested chrome
entries.reason: section heading

entries.text:
*Man & Machine* has no separate resale rule for used implants, so sell them
the same way as any other loot. Use the [fencing rules](../gear-and-fencing/#fencing-the-loot)
*(SR3 p.237–238)*: a **30%** base, **5% per net success** on the
Negotiation, never below **10%** or above **50%**. Stolen chrome isn't
standard gear, so expect the Finding a Fence TN to rise.

pdf.quote: The base price for most loot is 30 percent of its actual value
If the team won, the payment price will not rise above 50 percent of the actual value

entries.note: Resale of harvested chrome goes through the fencing rules, which are not built (see gear-and-fencing.md #43-70). The example arithmetic checks: 2,500 + 11,500 = 14,000; 30% = 4,200; 10% = 1,400; 50% = 7,000.

entries.text:
**Example.** A dead samurai's **smartlink** (2,500¥) and **retractable
spur** (11,500¥) *(SR3 p.302)* list at **14,000¥** together. The fence's
base offer is **4,200¥**. Depending on the Negotiation, the deal can't go
below 1,400¥ or above 7,000¥.

pdf.quote: The base price for most loot is 30 percent of its actual value
If the team won, the payment price will not rise above 50 percent of the actual value

entries.text:
# Buying Gear & Fencing
{: .no_toc }
entries.reason: page title / description / table of contents / horizontal rule / index page

entries.text:
Availability, Street Index and Legality Codes; buying through contacts; and
selling stolen goods to a fence. All rules are from the core rulebook,
*(SR3 p.237–238, p.270–274)*.

pdf.quote: Availability is a measure of how easy it is to obtain the item on the street

entries.text:
1. TOC
{:toc}
entries.reason: page title / description / table of contents / horizontal rule / index page

entries.text:
{: .fixed }
> Original gist: "Gear Availability, Acquisition, & Fencing Guide".
> - SR3 Legality Codes look like **`6P-E`**, not "R" or "F". The number is
>   the restriction level, **P** means a permit is available, and the letter
>   is the category.
> - Successes on the acquisition test **divide** the base time. They don't
>   cut it by 25–50% each.
> - Paying to hurry a search costs **+2 days and +0.1 Street Index for each
>   −1 to the Availability TN**. It's not "+25–50% per die".
> - The price is **negotiated**: Negotiation against Intelligence, **5% per
>   net success**.
> - Fencing: the **30% base and 5% per net success** were right, but the
>   limits are a **10% floor and a 50% ceiling**, not 60%. The "chop shop 10–15%"
>   rate and the hot, encrypted and scarce percentage modifiers were invented.
>   The book handles risk through the **Finding a Fence** TN instead.
> - The **Ares Predator III** isn't in the core rulebook. The examples below
>   use the core **Ares Predator** (450¥, Availability 3/24 hrs, Street
>   Index .5).

pdf.quote: Whichever side wins the Negotiation Test alters the price paid in his or her favor by 5 percent per extra success
If the fence won, the payment price will not drop below 10 percent of the actual value

entries.note: Composite errata callout. What is implemented (Availability as TN / base time, successes dividing the time, −1 TN for 2 days and +0.1 Street Index, negotiation at 5% per net success) is checked at #9, #16-20. pdf.quote: Each piece of gear has an individual description and a table listing

entries.text: | Statistic | Meaning |

entries.text: | **Availability** | Two numbers: **TN / base time**, for example `3/24 hrs`. |

pdf.quote: The number to the left is a target number that represents the difficulty of obtaining the item; the one to the right represents the base time necessary to acquire it

entries.text: | **Cost** | The legal retail price in nuyen. |

pdf.quote: Cost is the base cost of the weapon in nuyen

entries.text: | **Street Index** | The black-market multiplier on Cost. |

pdf.quote: Street Index is the market value multiplier to the item's base cost

entries.text: | **Legality** | Restriction level, permit availability, and category. |

pdf.quote: Legality represents whether or not it is illegal to own the item, carry or transport it, what restriction category it falls into, and whether or not permits for the item are available

Availability above **8**. *(SR3 p.270)* Gear modified for a dwarf costs

entries.text: ## Buying on the street  *(SR3 p.272–273)*

pdf.quote: characters must use an appropriate contact

entries.text:
1. **Find a source.** Contact a fixer or other suitable contact and make an
   **Etiquette Test** against the **Availability TN**. Contacts differ: a
   talismonger is great for magical goods and poor for guns.

pdf.quote: the player gets in touch with a contact (usually a fixer) and makes an Etiquette Test
Talismongers, for example, are an ideal contact for magical items, but not very good at acquiring weapons

code.snippet: talismonger:  { good: ['focus', 'spell', 'magical'], bad: ['firearm', 'melee', 'projectile', 'ammunition'], note: 'ideal for magical items, poor for weapons (p.272)' },

entries.text:
2. **Wait.** **Base time ÷ successes** is how long it takes the source to
   find the item.

pdf.quote: The base time divided by the number of successes provides the actual time it takes the source to locate the item

entries.text:
3. **No successes?** The contact can't or won't find it. At the GM's
   discretion you can put the word out: **for each −1 to the Availability
   TN, add 2 days to the wait and +0.1 to the Street Index**. *(SR3 p.273)*

pdf.quote: the character may add 2 days to the acquisition time period and .1 to the Street Index (increasing the cost) in order to reduce the Availability target number by 1

code.snippet: export const REDUCTION = { daysPerPoint: 2, streetIndexPerPoint: 0.1, page: 'SR3 p.272' };

entries.text:
4. **Negotiate.** Halfway through the wait you meet the source. The asking
   price is **Cost × Street Index**, plus any increase from step 3. You and
   the source each roll **Negotiation against the other's Intelligence**.
   The winner moves the price **5% per net success** in their favor.
   *(SR3 p.273)*

pdf.quote: Halfway through this period, face-to-face negotiations to determine the actual cost take place
pitting their Negotiations Skill Ratings against each other's Intelligence

code.snippet: return { time, halfway: time / 2, found: true };

entries.text:
5. **Pick up.** If you won't pay, the deal is off, and the GM may raise the
   Availability TN next time you use that contact. *(SR3 p.273)*

pdf.quote: gamemasters can adjust the Availability target number upward the next time the character searches for something through that contact

entries.note: The deal being off if you won't pay is a card nobody presses (nothing is charged until 💴). Raising the Availability TN for that contact next time is not tracked.

entries.text: ### The book's example  *(SR3 p.273)*

pdf.quote: She wants to buy it on the street. The whip has an Availability of 24/14 days, with a Street Index of 3

entries.text:
Cheshire wants a **monofilament whip**: Availability **24/14 days**,
Street Index **3**, Cost **3,000¥**. None of her contacts come close to TN

pdf.quote: That means she'll be waiting 24 extra days (2 x 12 = 24)
That makes the cost a whopping 12,600

entries.text:
24. She puts the word out, cutting the TN to **12**. That adds **24 days**
(2 × 12) and **+1.2** Street Index. She rolls 2 successes: (24 + 14) ÷ 2 =
**19 days**. The price is 3,000 × 4.2 = **12,600¥**. She wins the
negotiation by 4, which is 20% off, and pays **10,080¥**.

pdf.quote: That means she'll be waiting 24 extra days (2 x 12 = 24)
That makes the cost a whopping 12,600

pdf.quote: If a shadowrunning team has a prearranged deal for disposing of loot, then the following rules do not apply

apply. Otherwise, you need a fence.

pdf.quote: Finding a fence requires a successful Etiquette (Street) Test. The Base Target Number is 4

entries.text:
{: .fixed }
> Original gist: "Life with a SIN vs. Living SINless".
> - The **Fake SIN price table was invented**. In SR3 a fake ID is a forged
>   credstick, and its rating sets its price: **Rating × Rating × 1,000¥** at
>   ratings 1–4, rising steeply after that. The table is below.
> - A SIN is not a "12-digit alphanumeric code". The book says the number is
>   **generated from personal data**, and police can read your birth date,
>   state of origin and initials from it.
> - "30–40% of the population is SINless" appears in no SR3 book checked.
> - There's no "Lesser / Greater Magical Permit". In the UCAS and CAS, magic
>   of **Force 3 or more** is regulated and needs a permit. Unregistered
>   spells, spirits and foci fall under legality category **(T) Class E
>   Magic**.
> - Permits **require a valid SIN**, and a fake one must beat a Rating 6
>   verification system.

entries.text: ## How the corps got above the law  *(SR3 p.22)*
entries.reason: Setting fact, no code counterpart; checked against SR3 p.22 (heading: "And So It Came to Pass ..." section on the Seretech and Shiawase decisions): agrees. The page opens its account of "two Supreme Court rulings, made in 1999 and 2001".

entries.text:
Two US Supreme Court rulings at the turn of the century made the modern
megacorp:
entries.reason: Lore, no page cited; checked against SR3 p.22 ("The kickoff came with two Supreme Court rulings, made in 1999 and 2001"): agrees.

entries.text:
- **The Seretech decision** upheld a corporation's right to keep an
  **armed force** to protect its people and property. That legitimised
  private corporate armies.
entries.reason: Lore, no page cited; checked against SR3 p.22 (Seretech: "upheld Seretech Corporation's right to maintain an armed force for the protection of its personnel and property"): agrees.

entries.text:
- **The Shiawase decision** established **corporate extraterritoriality**:
  a multinational gets the same rights and privileges as a foreign
  government. Its land is effectively foreign soil.
entries.reason: Lore, no page cited; checked against SR3 p.22 (Shiawase: "established corporate extraterritoriality, giving multinational corporations the same rights and privileges as foreign governments"): agrees.

entries.text:
The rest follows from those two rulings. A corp facility is a sovereign
enclave with its own army, so the police can't simply walk in, and no
government can easily make a corp answer for anything.
entries.reason: Guide's summary of the consequence of the two rulings; an inference, states no rule.

entries.text:
The SR3 introduction sums up the result. Megacorps are "a law unto
themselves", the nuyen is the world's currency, and when a corp wants a job
done without dirtying its hands, it hires shadowrunners *(SR3 p.8)*.
entries.reason: Setting fact, no code counterpart; checked against SR3 p.8: agrees. Quotes "a law unto themselves", the nuyen as global monetary standard, and "When the megacorps want a job done but don't want to dirty their hands, they need a shadowrun".

## The Corporate Court: the referee
{: #the-corporate-court-the-referee }
entries.reason: heading / navigation / table header / divider - states no rule

entries.text:
The biggest corps answer, loosely, to one body: the **Corporate Court**,
which they sit on themselves.
entries.reason: Lore, no page cited; checked against NS p.83 and SR3 p.31 (the Corporate Court, which the Big Eight sit on): agrees.

entries.text:
- **It owns the bank.** In 2032–33 the Court took over Global Financial
  Services, which had replaced the World Bank. It moved GFS into orbit as
  the **Zurich-Orbital Gemeinschaft Bank** *(SR3 p.31)*.
entries.reason: Setting fact, no code counterpart; checked against SR3 p.31 (Show Me the Money, 2032-2033): agrees. Quotes "The Corporate Court takes over Global Financial Services. It moves GFS to the Zurich-Orbital Habitat and renames it the Zurich-Orbital Gemeinschaft Bank"; the 2020 entry says GFS replaced the World Bank.

entries.text:
- **It acts for the corps together.** In 2048 Aztlan nationalised every
  foreign business. The corps answered with **Operation Reciprocity**, a
  combined corporate military strike on Aztechnology troops in Ensenada.
  The **Veracruz Settlement** that followed compensated the other corps and
  let them back into Aztlan, provided Aztlan citizens held the major
  shares of their local subsidiaries. The same year, the **Panama Canal** became a
  Pan-Corporate Zone under the Court's authority *(SR3 p.31)*.
entries.reason: Setting fact, no code counterpart; checked against SR3 p.31 (2048 entry): agrees. Operation Reciprocity, the Veracruz Settlement (Aztlan-citizen major shareholders of "foreign" subsidiaries) and the Panama Canal as a Pan-Corporate Zone under the Corporate Court all match.

entries.text:
- **A seat on it is fiercely contested.** Yamatetsu spent 2041 fighting for
  a seat on the Court and on the Zurich-Orbital board. When it won, the
  "Big Seven" became the **Big Eight** *(SR3 p.31)*. In 2059 suborbital
  **Flight 1118** from Tokyo crashed into the Redmond Barrens, killing
  Fuchi's Court representative, David Hague. His seat went not to a Big
  Eight corp but to **Wuxing**, a family corp made rich by Dunkelzahn's will
  *(SR3 p.35)*.
entries.reason: Setting fact, no code counterpart; checked against SR3 p.31 (Yamatetsu, Big Seven to Big Eight, 2041-42) and SR3 p.35 (Flight 1118, 2059; David Hague; Wuxing): agrees. The book dates Flight 1118 and the Hague seat to 2059, so this is not a later-event problem.

entries.text:
**What that means for runners:** the Court keeps corp-on-corp fighting
**deniable**. An open war risks the others ganging up on you, as they did on
Aztlan. A shadowrun that nobody can trace doesn't.
entries.reason: "What that means for runners" - GM-facing inference; states no rule.

entries.text: ### Corps in one city: the United Corporate Council  *(NS p.83)*
entries.reason: Setting fact, no code counterpart; checked against NS p.83 (United Corporate Council): agrees.

entries.text:
Seattle's corps present one face to the city government through the
**United Corporate Council**. It's an advisory body to the governor that
pushes the corporate agenda. It was formed in 2030, after a corp war in
which Aztechnology wiped out Campana & Carrindum, so that such
"misunderstandings" wouldn't happen again. *New Seattle* calls it a
small-scale version of the Corporate Court. Its members include the
megacorps, the big local corps, Lone Star and the Draco Foundation. The
backstabbing inside it is constant but subtle. A member that moves too
openly risks the rest ganging up on it, so they hire runners for
**paydata**, to give their lobbyists an edge.

entries.text:
- **Ask who gains.** Most runs in these books trace back to one faction
  hurting another. Before a run, decide who the Johnson really works for,
  which rival is the real target, and who else is watching. The Johnson
  types are covered in *(MJLBB p.17–18)*.

### The Draco Foundation
{: #the-draco-foundation }
entries.reason: heading / navigation / table header / divider - states no rule

entries.text:
Set up by Dunkelzahn's will to administer his bequests, with Nadja Daviar
as chair *(SR3 p.34)*. In Seattle it is run by **Sassinian**, a sasquatch.
The Council of Princes refused it an office in the Tir, so the Seattle
office covers the Tir as well. *New Seattle* calls it "a big-big-big
employer of shadowrunners": it has plenty of money and a will to carry out
*(NS p.91–92)*. It also sits on the UCC *(NS p.83)*.
entries.reason: Setting fact, no code counterpart; checked against SR3 p.34 and NS pp.83, 91-92: agrees. Dunkelzahn's will provided for the Draco Foundation, "with Daviar as chairman of the board"; Sassinian is "a Salish-area sasquatch"; the Council of Princes refused an office; "The Draco Foundation is a big-big-big employer of shadowrunners"; a Draco Foundation member of the UCC (Morgan Gallagher).

entries.text: ### Fuchi Industrial Electronics  *(SR3 p.34–35)*
entries.reason: Setting fact, no code counterpart; checked against SR3 pp.34-35 (Fuchi): agrees.

entries.text:
A Big Eight computer giant tearing itself apart. Fuchi has **three internal
factions**, and the corp war with Renraku has made their feud worse. In
mid-2059 Fuchi accused Renraku of stealing its secrets through Miles Lanier,
its former security chief; the charges were dropped. **Richard Villiers**,
expecting the other factions to force him out, has formed **Novatech** and
is quietly buying his Fuchi North America holdings into it. He has offered
Lanier the job of Novatech's head of security. Every faction, and every
rival, wants to know what happens to Fuchi next, which means steady work
for runners.
entries.reason: Lore, no page cited beyond the heading; checked against SR3 pp.34-35: Fuchi's "three internal factions"; "Around mid-2059, Fuchi formally accused Renraku of industrial espionage with the aid of Miles Lanier. The charges were eventually dropped"; Villiers formed Novatech and "offered his old buddy Miles Lanier the job of Head of Security". All dated 2059 or earlier: agrees.

entries.text: ### Mitsuhama Computer Technologies  *(NS p.92–93)*
entries.reason: Setting fact, no code counterpart; checked against NS pp.92-93 (Mitsuhama): agrees.

entries.text:
It aims for the top spot in computing while Fuchi and Renraku fight.
Runners credit it with the **"zero-zone"**: zero penetration, zero
survival. That means concealed autoguns, lethal gas, barghest guard dogs,
bound elementals, and **black ice** that kills. Its wage mages are
**Unit 13**, which is mostly human, with no shamans. Its Johnsons want the
job done exactly as planned. For its "special problems" it can call on the
Seattle yakuza.
entries.reason: Setting fact, deliberate for the campaign date. NS pp.92-93 says Mitsuhama "In the past" called on the Seattle yakuza, before their secession; New Seattle dates the secession only by its 2060 posts. The maintainer's GM-only journal (packs-src/sr3e-gm-sixth-world/the-sixth-world-after-october-2059-gm-only.*.json, "The yakuza break with Japan") places it after October 2059, the date these pages describe, so the guide's present tense is right for that date (checked 2026-10-18).

entries.text: ### Renraku Computer Systems  *(SR3 p.34–35)*
entries.reason: Setting fact, no code counterpart; checked against SR3 pp.34-35 (Renraku): agrees.

entries.text:
Fuchi's great rival, and lately the winner: months after Miles Lanier
joined its board in 2058, Renraku began producing remarkable technological
advances. Fuchi's espionage charges in mid-2059 were dropped, but Lanier
left Renraku and sold his stock to the Zurich-Orbital bank. In Seattle,
Renraku is the **Arcology**: a self-contained corporate city that houses
nearly 100,000 people *(NS p.30)*.
entries.reason: Setting fact, no code counterpart; checked against SR3 pp.34-35 and NS p.30: agrees. Lanier's 2058 seat and Renraku's advances "just months after Lanier joined the board" (SR3 p.34); mid-2059 charges dropped, Lanier sold his Renraku stock to the Zurich-Orbital Bank (SR3 p.35); the arcology holds "nearly 100,000 inhabitants" (NS p.30). The December 2059 lockdown is not mentioned, correctly for October 2059.

entries.text: ### Saeder-Krupp  *(SR3 p.31; NS p.94–95)*
entries.reason: Setting fact, no code counterpart; checked against SR3 p.31 and NS pp.94-95 (Saeder-Krupp): agrees.

entries.text:
Owned by the great dragon **Lofwyr**, and called the world's largest
megacorp. Officially it has no presence in Seattle. Unofficially it has
subsidiaries, small offices, and watchers posted by Lofwyr. "The biggest
business Saeder-Krupp does in Seattle is shadow business," and nobody can
predict what it will want.
entries.reason: Lore, no page cited beyond the heading; checked against NS p.95: "the world's largest megacorporation"; "Seattle Division: None (officially)"; subsidiaries, innocuous offices and watchers; "The biggest business Saeder-Krupp does in Seattle is shadow business"; "With Lofwyr, you can never tell": agrees.

entries.text: ### Shiawase  *(NS p.76, p.95–96)*
entries.reason: Setting fact, no code counterpart; checked against NS p.76 and pp.95-96 (Shiawase): agrees.

entries.text:
The Shiawase decision that created extraterritoriality is named after this
corp *(SR3 p.22)*. Shiawase Atomics maintains Seattle's power grid, and
wants Gaeatronics's generating contract *(NS p.76)*. Its spy network often
knows a run is coming. Its defences use **net-guns and knockout gas**, and
its ice is mostly trace, because it wants prisoners to interrogate.
entries.reason: Setting fact, no code counterpart; checked against SR3 p.22 and NS pp.76, 95-97: agrees. The Shiawase decision followed a botched attack on a Shiawase, Inc. nuclear plant (SR3 p.22); Shiawase Atomics maintains the grid and wants the generating contract (NS p.76); intelligence network "more often than not the corp knows about it"; net-guns and knockout gas; ice is "trace and maybe some deck-burning drek" (NS p.95-96).

entries.text: ### Wuxing  *(SR3 p.35; NS p.81, p.96)*
entries.reason: Setting fact, no code counterpart; checked against SR3 p.35 and NS p.81, p.96 (Wuxing): agrees.

entries.text:
A small family corp until Dunkelzahn's money raised it to the top. In 2059
Wuxing took the Corporate Court seat left empty when Fuchi's representative
died *(SR3 p.35)*. It drives the **Pacific Prosperity Group**, a trade bloc
against Japanese economic dominance. That makes it an enemy of the Japanese
corps, and a rival of Federated-Boeing, which is also in the PPG. Runners
expect the **Triads** to work on its behalf.
entries.reason: Setting fact, no code counterpart; checked against SR3 p.35 and NS pp.81, 96: agrees. A "mom-and-pop corp jumped up to the big time" by Dunkelzahn's cash; Hague's Court seat; PPG formed "to break the Japanese economic stranglehold on the Pac Rim"; not endeared to the Japanacorps; Federated-Boeing "also a member of the PPG"; a runner predicts Triad action on Wuxing's behalf.

entries.text: ### Yamatetsu  *(SR3 p.35; NS p.96)*
entries.reason: Setting fact, no code counterpart; checked against SR3 p.35 and NS p.96 (Yamatetsu): agrees.

entries.text:
When chairman Tadamako Shibanokuji died in 2059, his shares went to his son

headquarters to **Vladivostok** *(SR3 p.35)*. It now sells itself as the
meta-friendly, "Awakened" corp, and its traditionalist staff are fighting
that change. It has no friends among the other Japanese corps *(NS p.96)*.
entries.reason: Setting fact, no code counterpart; checked against SR3 p.35 and NS p.96: agrees. Chairman Tadamako Shibanokuji died in 2059, shares reverted to his ork son Yuri, HQ moved to Vladivostok (SR3 p.35); "Yamatetsu has no friends among the Japanacorps" (NS p.96).

entries.text:
# Politics, Police & Policlubs
{: .no_toc }
entries.reason: heading / navigation / table header / divider - states no rule

entries.text:
Who enforces the law, who lobbies and bombs for a cause, and how Seattle
deals with its neighbours, as of October 2059. These are the powers that
aren't megacorps or syndicates, but deal with both.

entries.text:
## Law enforcement is a business
{: #law-enforcement-is-a-business }
entries.reason: heading / navigation / table header / divider - states no rule

entries.text:
Seattle fired its whole police department in **2025**, after the officers
went on strike, and gave policing to **Lone Star** *(SR3 p.28; NS p.76)*.
Police work is now "a business like any other" *(NS p.76)*.
entries.reason: Setting fact, no code counterpart; checked against SR3 p.28 and NS p.76: agrees. SR3 p.28: "Lone Star took over law enforcement in the Seattle Metroplex in 2025, after the Seattle Police Department had the bad judgment to go on strike. The governor declared the strike illegal, fired them all and hired the cop corp"; NS p.76: "the law in Seattle has become a business like any other".

entries.text: | Provider | Owner and base | Role in Seattle |
entries.reason: heading / navigation / table header / divider - states no rule

entries.text: | **Lone Star Security Services** | Austin, Texas | **The** police, under city contract. It has authority over every other security corp in the metroplex *(NS p.76, p.78)*. |
entries.reason: Setting fact, no code counterpart; checked against NS p.76 and p.78: agrees. Lone Star, HQ Austin, Texas, is "the official provider of policing to the Seattle metroplex"; p.78: "Lone Star has authority over all other security corps in the metroplex".

entries.text: | **Knight Errant** | Ares (Damien Knight's own project), Detroit | Second-largest provider. It holds private contracts and has a training academy in Renton. Its image is elite, while Lone Star's is "beat cops" *(NS p.77)*. |
entries.reason: Setting fact, no code counterpart; checked against NS p.77: agrees. Knight Errant: Detroit, "The brainchild and pet project of Ares CEO Damien Knight", "Seattle's second-largest security provider", training academy in Renton, KE personnel "considered elite" against Lone Star's "beat cops".

entries.text: | **Eagle Security, Hard Corps, Wolverine** and others | Various | At least twenty firms in all. They may act only on their client's property, and must hold a suspect there until Lone Star arrives *(NS p.78)*. |
entries.reason: Setting fact, no code counterpart; checked against NS p.78: agrees. "At least twenty different private security providers operate in Seattle ... Eagle Security, Hard Corps, Inc. and Wolverine Security"; the other corps "can only take action on a customer's site, and keep a perp from escaping until Lone Star shows up".

entries.text:
- **The contract is always contested.** Knight Errant wants Lone Star's
  contract, and so does the Sioux-based Eagle Security, though the city is
  unlikely to trust a NAN corp *(NS p.76)*.
entries.reason: Setting fact, no code counterpart; checked against NS p.76: agrees. Knight Errant "would love to get hold of that big, juicy city contract"; Sioux-based Eagle Security "wouldn't mind getting it either", but "it's hard to imagine the government trusting a NAN-based corp".

entries.text:
- **The police hire runners too.** Lone Star Seattle's **Shadowriders** are
  a covert unit that hires freelance runners for not-quite-legal jobs against
  the syndicates, and has people ready to take the blame if a job goes wrong
  *(NS p.76)*.
entries.reason: Setting fact, no code counterpart; checked against NS p.76: agrees. "he recently re-established the Shadowriders, a covert black-ops division of Lone Star Seattle"; Marrs "has saps in place to take the fall if necessary".

entries.text:
- **The "Dips"**, Lone Star's magical investigation division (DPI), read
  crime scenes astrally and **license Seattle's legal magicians**. That
  gives them leverage over above-ground magic *(NS p.77)*.
entries.reason: Setting fact, no code counterpart; checked against NS p.77: agrees. The "Dips" (Department of Magical Investigation, DPI) investigate "all crimes involving magic", read crime scenes astrally, and "Lone Star controls the licensing and certification of magicians in Seattle".

entries.text: ### The Metroplex Guard  *(NS p.78)*
entries.reason: Setting fact, no code counterpart; checked against NS p.78 (the military: the Metroplex Guard): agrees.

entries.text:
Seattle's own military is the **Metroplex Guard**. It has quietly kept
metahumans out of its ranks, and it's an open secret that **Humanis**
recruits from it: some Guard officers and senior NCOs hold posts in Humanis.
entries.reason: Setting fact, no code counterpart; checked against NS p.78: agrees. The Guard "has a lot of leeway in choosing who gets in ... resulted in a 'weeding out' of metahumans"; "It's an open secret that the Humanis Policlub recruits from the Metroplex Guard, and a few officers and senior NCOs also hold key positions in Humanis". The Joint Task Force Seattle material on the same page follows the Renraku lockdown (December 2059) and the guide correctly leaves it out.

entries.text:
## Policlubs
{: #policlubs }
entries.reason: heading / navigation / table header / divider - states no rule

entries.text:
*New Seattle* sorts policlubs into three camps: anti-Awakened and
anti-metahuman, pro-metahuman, and pro-civil rights. It also sorts them by
type: **political and fraternal organisations**, **terrorist groups**, and
a rumoured third kind, secretive circles of the wealthy *(NS p.79)*.
entries.reason: Setting fact, no code counterpart; checked against NS p.79: agrees. "Policlubs fall into three broad camps: anti-Awakened/anti-metahuman, pro-metahuman, and generally pro-civil rights and liberties"; two types, "political/fraternal organizations and terrorist groups"; "A third type of group does exist, but in such a shadowy and unsubstantiated way that they are generally dismissed as rumors" (the Human Nation).

entries.text: | Policlub | Leader in Seattle | Stance | Backing and links |
entries.reason: heading / navigation / table header / divider - states no rule

entries.text: | **Humanis Policlub** | Karl Brackhaven | Human supremacist. Treats metahumanity as a disease. | Founded **2023** *(SR3 p.28)*. Publicly it only lobbies. Privately it **fronts for and funds** terrorists such as **Alamos 20,000** and the **Hand of Five**, and steers its most violent members to them *(NS p.79–80)*. |
entries.reason: Setting fact, no code counterpart; checked against SR3 p.28 and NS pp.79-80: agrees. SR3 p.28: "the founding of the Humanis Policlub ... in 2023"; NS p.79: Leader Karl Brackhaven; "they quietly fund such associations as Alamos 20,000, the Hand of Five and other terrorist groups"; "Humanis draws in members and quietly diverts the most violent and virulent to Alamos 20K and their ilk"; treats metahumanity "as a disease rather than a natural state of being".

entries.text: | **Ork Rights Commission (ORC)** | Jasper Squashright | Metahuman rights, focused on orks | Grassroots, but runners say it has a real war chest and pays runners well. Runners also claim its leaders pass resources to pro-Awakened terrorists such as the **Sons of Sauron** *(NS p.80)*. |
entries.reason: Setting fact, no code counterpart; checked against NS p.80: agrees. Leader Jasper Squashright; "grassroots metahuman-rights organization, mostly devoted to the cause of orks"; a runner says ORC "have a pretty decent war chest" and pays well; another says ORC bigwigs "slide information and resources" to pro-Awakened groups "like the Sons of Sauron and the Children of the Sixth World" - runners' posts, as the guide says.

entries.text: | **Empowerment Coalition** | Libby Chalmers | Civil rights | Funded by Dunkelzahn's **Timmons Memorial Fund**. It is bringing ORC and other groups under its umbrella, and will pay runners *(NS p.80)*. |
entries.reason: Setting fact, no code counterpart; checked against NS p.80: agrees. Leader Libby Chalmers; the Timmons Memorial Fund from Dunkelzahn's will; the Coalition "has been helping groups like ORC and Mothers of Metahumans"; a runner says Chalmers "is more than willing to spend Coalition money on shadowrunners".

entries.text:
**How they interact:** Humanis has rich friends. **Kenneth Brackhaven**, an
investor and Karl Brackhaven's nephew, heads Brackhaven Investments (whose
seat on the UCC is held by Norman Jones) and has contributed to the
campaigns of at least six district mayors *(NS p.83–84)*. The Coalition's
Libby Chalmers reportedly faced him down when he told her the Coalition
wasn't wanted in Seattle *(NS p.80)*. Each side's terrorists are its
deniable hand, much as shadowrunners are the corps'.
entries.reason: Setting fact, no code counterpart; checked against NS p.83-84: Kenneth Brackhaven, Karl's nephew, heads Brackhaven Investments (UCC seat Norman Jones) and contributed to the campaigns of at least six district mayors: agrees since the 0.7.0 wording fix (68d39066).

entries.text:
{: .note }
> **The Human Nation** appears in two ways. NS p.79 names it in the rumoured
> third category, a circle of the very rich funding experiments on
> metahumans. NS p.80 then lists it among Humanis's terrorist fronts.
> The book leaves the contradiction unresolved.
entries.reason: Setting fact, no code counterpart; checked against NS p.79: agrees. The Human Nation is named as the example of the rumoured third kind of group, and the sentence "Humanis operates as a front organization for anti-Awakened terrorist groups like Alamos 20,000, Human Nation, the Hand of Five and others" starts at the foot of p.79 and ends at the top of p.80. The guide's "NS p.80 then lists it" is accurate for the second half of that sentence.

entries.text:
## Foreign relations
{: #foreign-relations }
entries.reason: heading / navigation / table header / divider - states no rule

entries.text:
Seattle is a UCAS city surrounded by NAN territory. Since 2042 it has been
allowed to send its own envoys abroad *(NS p.80)*. Its position goes back
to the Treaty of Denver, which kept cities like Seattle as extraterritorial
extensions of their governments *(SR3 p.27)*.
entries.reason: Setting fact, no code counterpart; checked against NS p.80 and SR3 p.27: agrees. NS p.80: "In 2042, the UCAS granted Seattle the right to send its own representatives to any nations considered vital to its survival"; SR3 p.27: the Treaty of Denver provided "the maintenance of cities like Seattle as extraterritorial extensions of various governments".

entries.text: | Neighbour | Relations  *(NS p.81)* |

entries.reason: Setting fact, no code counterpart; checked against NS p.81: agrees. Seattle's ties with Korea have grown; "Wuxing, Inc., the PPG's driving force, has already set up corporate offices in the metroplex".

entries.text: ### How the nations got here  *(SR3 p.27–30)*
entries.reason: Setting fact, no code counterpart; checked against SR3 pp.27-30 (history of the nations): agrees.

entries.text:
The Treaty of Denver gave the **Native American Nations** most of western
North America *(SR3 p.27)*. The **CAS** broke from the newly merged
UCAS in 2034. The elves founded **Tír na nÓg** (2034) and **Tir Tairngire**

California's 2036–37 collapse left **San Francisco** under Japanese
corporate control *(SR3 p.30)*.

{: .no_toc }

example the books give in most detail.

{: .note }
> *New Seattle*'s underworld chapter is written in character. The Mafia
> section is a stolen letter from a consigliere, and the Seoulpa section
> comes from leaked Lone Star files *(NS p.97–106)*. Treat the details as
> what those sources believe.
entries.reason: Setting fact, no code counterpart; checked against NS pp.97-106: agrees. The Mafia section is an intercepted report from consigliere "Uncle Al" Cavalieri to Rowena O'Malley (NS p.97-98); the Seoulpa section is "from Lone Star's secret files" (NS p.104). The latest dated post in the section is 28 September 2060.

entries.text: ## Why the syndicates matter
entries.reason: heading / navigation / table header / divider - states no rule

entries.text:
The SR3 introduction says the Mafia, the Yakuza and the other syndicates
"have grown explosively", because their networks supply anything people
will buy *(SR3 p.8)*. In Seattle, the city's position as a UCAS island
inside NAN territory, near the sea route to Russia, makes it a major
smuggling port for every syndicate *(NS p.82)*. The syndicates hire runners
through **street Johnsons**, who have less money than corp Johnsons but can
offer protection, illegal services or extra bodies *(MJLBB p.18)*.
entries.reason: Setting fact, no code counterpart; checked against SR3 p.8, NS p.82, MJLBB p.18: agrees. SR3 p.8: "The Mafia, Yakuza and other crime syndicates have grown explosively as their networks provide anything that people will buy"; NS p.82: Seattle's "status as an island of UCAS law in the middle of NAN territory, so close to the route across the strait to Russia" makes it a smuggling hub; MJLBB p.18: a street Johnson's "funding and resources are probably far less than a corporate Johnson's" but the group can offer "protection, illegal services or extra bodies".

entries.text: ## The Mafia  *(NS p.97–100)*
entries.reason: Setting fact, no code counterpart; checked against NS pp.97-100 (the Mafia): agrees.

entries.text:
It began on Seattle's docks and in its labour unions, and was run from
Chicago. Since O'Malley's death, **who will be capo of Seattle** is the
question of the moment. His daughter **Rowena O'Malley** took over the
Finnigan Family within days and made a strong bid for it; **Maurice
"Butcher" Bigio** is the other contender. The O'Malley camp believes Bigio
arranged O'Malley's death *(NS p.97–98, p.100)*.
entries.reason: Setting fact, deliberate for the campaign date. NS p.97 reports the Commissione appointing Bigio capo of Seattle, in posts dated September 2060 with no date for the appointment. The GM-only journal (packs-src/sr3e-gm-sixth-world/the-sixth-world-after-october-2059-gm-only.*.json, "The Mafia: Bigio becomes capo") places it after October 2059, so the guide's "who will be capo … is the question of the moment" is right for that date. The guide's cite for "arranged O'Malley's death" should include NS p.98.

entries.text: ## The Yakuza  *(NS p.100–102)*
entries.reason: Setting fact, no code counterpart; checked against NS pp.100-102 (the yakuza): agrees.

entries.text:
The yakuza followed the Japanese corps to Seattle. The Seattle clans answer
to **Hanzo Shotozumi**, who was made oyabun of Seattle by **Akira Watada**
of the powerful **Watada-rengo** in Japan and told to rebuild a traditional,
loyal organisation. Since O'Malley's death they have become the most
powerful syndicate in the Pacific Northwest, and Shotozumi's ambition has
grown with them *(NS p.101)*.
entries.reason: Setting fact, no code counterpart; checked against NS p.101: agrees. The yakuza arrived with the Japanese corporations; Watada chose Shotozumi to "rebuild a traditional and loyal yakuza organization"; "The growth of the yakuza over the years made them the most powerful syndicate in the Pacific Northwest" - the book attributes this to their long growth and adds that they seized markets after O'Malley's death in 2058, so the guide's "Since O'Malley's death" compresses it. The guide does not mention that Shotozumi then split from the Watada-rengo (the Shotozumi-rengo), which the book also states.

entries.text: ## The Triads  *(NS p.102–104)*
entries.reason: Setting fact, no code counterpart; checked against NS pp.102-104 (the Triads): agrees.

entries.text:
Chinese syndicates that control Hong Kong and most of mainland China. In
Seattle they're junior to the Mafia and the Yakuza, but rising: the city
leans toward the PPG, which is opening trade with Hong Kong. Most of their
money comes from **smuggling**. The Triads take metahumans and women more
readily than other syndicates do *(NS p.102; MJLBB p.54)*.
entries.reason: Setting fact, no code counterpart; checked against NS p.102 and MJLBB p.54: agrees. NS p.102: Chinese syndicates "control Hong Kong and most of mainland China", "overshadowed by the yakuza and the Mafia in Seattle", PPG "opening trade to Hong Kong", "make most of their money in smuggling"; the Yellow Lotus recruits "metahumans barred from joining other criminal gangs"; MJLBB p.54: "the Triads are more enlightened than most other organized crime groups regarding the membership of women and metahumans".

entries.text: ## Gangs
entries.reason: heading / navigation / table header / divider - states no rule

entries.text:
Below the syndicates are the street gangs, often allied with them. The
**Tigers** work with the Eighty-Eights *(NS p.103)*. The all-elf
**Ancients** control smuggling from the Tir *(NS p.106)*. *New Seattle*
covers the major gangs from p.106 onward, and each district's gangs in its
district chapters.
entries.reason: Setting fact, no code counterpart; checked against NS p.103 and p.106: agrees. The Eighty-Eights "forged an alliance with the Tigers" (NS p.103); the Ancients, "an all-elf go-gang", control "smuggling from Salem and Portland into Seattle" (NS p.106); the gang write-ups begin on p.106 ("TOP GANGS").
